To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the flight test data was insufficient for analysis, 2) the flight test points were non-repeatably acquired, 3) the flight test instrumentation was limited, and 4) the data was insufficient to address the analysis objectives.

the flight test data can be extended and the challenges addressed using mathematical models and cycle decks to predict the uninstalled engine performance and the effects of the inlet temperature distortion and biased inlet temperature measurement on engine scheduling.

flight test data can be used to validate mathematical models, engine performance models can be used to extend flight test data, and computational fluid dynamics models can be used in lieu of flight test data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of mathematical models to the flight test and engine evaluation process.
developing a methodology to extend the usefulness and accuracy of flight test data.
understanding the effects of the temperature distortion and TT2 bias on engine scheduling and stability margin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

flight test data is the gold standard for propulsion system evaluation, but it can be augmented and enhanced by other data sources to provide the most complete and accurate picture of the propulsion system.

the use of mathematical models, cycle decks, ground test data and computational fluid dynamics, as well as a combination of these, are necessary to address the challenges of flight test analysis and evaluation of the aircraft propulsion system.
the challenges are significant and the solution methodologies are effective.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a methodology that allows us to use the limited flight test instrumentation to evaluate the propulsion system.
we were able to address all of the challenges with a combination of the available data and the techniques described.
a combination of ground testing, flight testing, and analysis techniques can be employed to evaluate the performance of the propulsion system in a flight environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to address many of the challenges using a combination of flight data and ground test data.
the flight test and ground test data must be integrated with models, computational fluid dynamics analysis, and other tools to fully understand the performance of the propulsion system.
the flight test data are often not sufficient to fully address the questions of interest.
